hints: Work backwards from the two products of U, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, and count carbons to find what functional group can give both.
walkthrough:
Track the carbon skeleton from both products**
Look beside you at Fig. 7.1. Both products from U contain two carbons, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. So U must also be a two carbon compound. That narrows things hugely.

Spot the functional group that does both jobs**
Reaction 2 uses $\text{LiAlH}_4$ to make a primary amine. Only a nitrile, $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$, reduces to $\text{R-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ like that. The same nitrile hydrolyses in reaction 1 to $\text{R-COOH}$. With $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3$, U is $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$, which contains only C, H and N, three elements.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$ / ethanenitrile

hints: Recall what type of hydrolysis converts a nitrile, $\text{R-CN}$, fully to a carboxylic acid rather than stopping at the amide.
walkthrough:
Recognise full hydrolysis to the acid**
Converting $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is hydrolysis, adding water across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond. To drive it all the way to the carboxylic acid you need dilute aqueous acid plus strong heating. Alkali would give the carboxylate salt, not the free acid.
Final answer: dilute aqueous acid, e.g. $\text{HCl(aq)}$, with heat

hints: Remember the standard product when $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ reacts with $\text{SOCl}_2$ in reaction 3.
walkthrough:
Convert OH into Cl**
$\text{SOCl}_2$ swaps the $\text{-OH}$ of a carboxylic acid for $\text{-Cl}$. So $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$. This is why V reacts so readily with the amine in reaction 5 with no special conditions, acyl chlorides are very reactive.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ / ethanoyl chloride

hints: Write the full equation for $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2$ and remember the two small gaseous byproducts formed alongside the acyl chloride.
walkthrough:
Balance the familiar equation**
Think of this as $\text{-OH}$ replaced by $\text{-Cl}$. The O and extra H and Cl go to $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{HCl} + \text{SO}_2$$ Check atoms, everything balances and you have the complete equation for reaction 3.

hints: Look at reaction 4 where W plus $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ gives $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$, and work out what ethyl-containing electrophile must supply the second ethyl group.
walkthrough:
Supply the second ethyl group**
The product $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ is a secondary amine with two identical ethyl groups. One comes from ethylamine itself. The other must come from W, so W must be an ethyl electrophile that the amine can attack. That is a haloethane, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ / $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ / bromoethane / chloroethane

hints: Recall the special solvent and pressure conditions needed when a primary amine reacts with a haloalkane to form a secondary amine.
walkthrough:
Create the right environment for N-alkylation**
Reaction 4 is nucleophilic substitution of a haloalkane by ethylamine. You heat the mixture in ethanol as solvent, not water, to keep the organic haloalkane dissolved. Because the haloalkane and amine are volatile, you seal the tube or apply pressure so reagents do not escape.
Final answer: heat in ethanol, under pressure / in a sealed tube

hints: Identify the functional group change in reaction 6 from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ and recall which strong reducing agent does this.
walkthrough:
Reduce the carbonyl inside the amide**
Look at reaction 6 closely. The $\text{C=O}$ of the amide $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ becomes $\text{CH}_2$ in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$. That is reduction of an amide to an amine, which needs the powerful hydride donor $\text{LiAlH}_4$. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is too weak for this.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ / lithium aluminium hydride

hints: Start with reaction 1, nitrile to carboxylic acid with water, and decide which reaction type name fits addition of water.
Consider reaction 2, nitrile plus hydride to amine, and think why Cambridge counts hydride addition as both addition and reduction.
Look at reactions 3, 4 and 5 where $\text{OH}$, $\text{Cl}$ or $\text{Br}$ leaves and a new group takes its place without change in oxidation state.
Place reaction 6, amide $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH}_2$, and check you have used numbers 1 to 6 to fill all four rows.
walkthrough:
Hydrolysis is reaction 1**
Reaction 1 adds water across $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to give $\text{COOH}$. That is hydrolysis.

Addition is reaction 2**
Reaction 2 adds hydride across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond to build the amine. In terms of bond change it is addition.

Reduction is reactions 2 and 6**
Both reaction 2, nitrile to amine, and reaction 6, amide $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH}_2$, gain hydrogen and lose oxygen or increase electron density at carbon. Both are reductions, so 2 counts in two categories.

Substitution is reactions 3, 4 and 5**
Reaction 3 swaps $\text{OH}$ for $\text{Cl}$, reaction 4 swaps halogen for $\text{N}$-ethylamino group, reaction 5 swaps $\text{Cl}$ for $\text{N}$-ethylamino group. All exchange one group for another with no net redox, so they are nucleophilic substitutions.
Final answer: hydrolysis: 1; addition: 2; reduction: 2, 6; substitution: 3, 4, 5

hints: Write the three species in order first by thinking which nitrogen lone pair is most tied up in resonance.
Recall the definition of a base as a proton acceptor and link it to availability of the lone pair on N.
Compare $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ with $\text{NH}_3$ by considering how ethyl groups push electron density toward N.
Explain why $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ is weakest by drawing the delocalisation of the N lone pair into the adjacent $\text{C=O}$.
walkthrough:
State the basicity order**
Picture accepting a proton. The easiest to protonate is diethylamine, then ammonia, then the amide is far weakest: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5 > \text{NH}_3 > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$$ Most basic on the left, least basic on the right.

Link basicity to the nitrogen lone pair**
Basicity means how readily the lone pair on N accepts $\text{H}^+$ to form $\text{N-H}^+$. The more electron dense and available that lone pair is, the stronger the base. All three have one lone pair on N, but its environment is very different.

Explain why the secondary amine beats ammonia**
Ethyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. Two ethyl groups in $\text{(C}_2\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{NH}$ push electron density onto N, making its lone pair more negative and more ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$ than the lone pair in $\text{NH}_3$, which has only H atoms attached.

Explain why the amide is very weak**
In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ the N is directly attached to $\text{C=O}$. The N lone pair overlaps with the $\pi$ system of the carbonyl and is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group. Because the lone pair is already partly shared, it is much less available to accept a proton, so amides are almost neutral.

Final answer: most basic $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ > $\text{NH}_3$ > $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ least basic
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair on N to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Amine is strongest due to positive inductive, electron donating effect of ethyl / alkyl groups increasing electron density on N.
Amide is weakest because N lone pair is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group, less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
